issues.legal_issue: A municipal valuation law that displaces rent-control restrictions permits annual rental value to be determined by a reasonable assessment of relevant circumstances rather than by an automatic cap at the standard rent or the rent received by the owner.
material_facts: The owner leased a nine-storeyed commercial building to a tenant at a monthly rent of Rs. 75,000, and the tenant sublet premises to sub-tenants.
The municipal authority assessed annual value by taking account of rent paid by the sub-tenants to the tenant.
The Municipal Assessment Tribunal instead fixed annual value on the basis of rent received by the owner.
The governing municipal valuation provision contained a non-obstante clause displacing the operation of rent-control legislation.
issues.conclusion: The municipal authority was not invariably limited by the standard rent or the rent actually received by the owner. It had to determine the reasonable annual rental value by considering all relevant circumstances, including the actual rent received by the owner, any standard rent, rent received by the tenant from sub-tenants, prevailing rents nearby, and the peculiar circumstances of the property.
issues.legal_principle: Section 174 of the Calcutta Municipal Corporation Act, 1980, read with Sections 193 and 194, governs valuation where the municipal law displaces rent-control restrictions. The Court distinguished the first group of cases, including Corporation of Calcutta v. Life Insurance Corporation of India, Corporation of Calcutta v. Padma Debi, Guntur Municipal Council v. Guntur Town Rate Payers' Association, and Dewan Daulat Rai Kapoor v. New Delhi Municipal Committee, where rent-control limits applied, from cases involving municipal provisions that displaced those limits, including Municipal Corporation, Indore v. Ratnaprabha, Assistant General Manager, Central Bank of India v. Commissioner, Municipal Corporation for the City of Ahmedabad, East India Commercial Co. Pvt. Ltd. v. Corporation of Calcutta, Balbir Singh v. MCD, Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation, Srikant Kashinath Jituri v. Corporation of the City of Belgaum, and Government Servant Cooperative House Building Society Ltd. v. Union of India. Even where rent-control limits are displaced, a determined fair rent may generally provide a reasonable guide, but it is not an inflexible ceiling; the valuation must reflect the circumstances of the case.

predicates.municipal_property_tax_valuation: A municipal authority is determining the rental value of land or a building for property taxation.
predicates.rent_restrictions_displaced: The applicable municipal valuation regime displaces rent-control restrictions when determining taxable rental value.
predicates.premises_sublet: A tenant has sublet all or part of premises leased from the owner.

issues.definition: When a municipal property-tax valuation concerns sublet premises and the valuation regime displaces rent restrictions, the annual value is determined by reasonably considering the relevant rental factors.

issues.legal_issue: Rent received by a tenant from sub-tenants may inform municipal annual valuation but cannot be treated as the sole criterion for that valuation.
material_facts: The building was leased by its owner to a tenant and was subsequently sublet.
The municipality relied on rent paid by sub-tenants to the tenant when assessing annual value.
The Tribunal excluded the sub-tenants' payments and used the rent received by the owner instead.
issues.conclusion: The rent received by the tenant from sub-tenants could not be excluded categorically, but neither could it alone determine annual value; it had to be considered along with the owner's rent and other relevant circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Section 174 of the Calcutta Municipal Corporation Act, 1980, requires determination of the gross annual rent reasonably expected at the time of assessment. Sections 193 and 194 address primary liability and apportionment of the consolidated rate. The Court held that the principles in Padma Debi and Life Insurance Corporation, which arose under municipal laws without the relevant non-obstante provision, did not justify excluding sub-tenancy receipts under Section 174. The decision in Ratnaprabha and the other cases concerning municipal laws that displace rent-control restrictions support assessment by reference to the applicable municipal law and all relevant circumstances.

predicates.municipal_property_tax_valuation: A municipal authority is determining the rental value of land or a building for property taxation.
predicates.premises_sublet: A tenant has sublet all or part of premises leased from the owner.

issues.definition: When a municipal property-tax valuation concerns sublet premises, rent received from sub-tenants is relevant to the valuation but is not its sole criterion.

issues.legal_issue: A tribunal reconsidering a municipal valuation appeal after supervisory review must assess all relevant circumstances rather than being restricted to the rent paid by sub-tenants.
material_facts: The High Court set aside the Tribunal's decision after finding that it had wrongly excluded the rent paid by sub-tenants to the tenant.
The High Court remanded the appeals but directed the Tribunal to take the sub-tenants' payments into consideration in assessing annual value.
The owner had also received rent from the tenant, and the Supreme Court held that other circumstances were relevant to the valuation.
issues.conclusion: The remand for reconsideration was proper, but the Tribunal could not be restricted to the sub-tenants' payments. It had to consider all relevant circumstances, including the rent received by the owner and the rent paid by sub-tenants; any excess amount paid could be recovered as provided by law.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 174 of the Calcutta Municipal Corporation Act, 1980, the Tribunal must determine the gross annual rent reasonably expected at the time of assessment by considering the relevant circumstances. Sections 193 and 194 govern liability for the consolidated rate and recovery of excess amounts. The Court applied its conclusions concerning the distinct municipal-law regimes discussed in Padma Debi, Life Insurance Corporation, Ratnaprabha, and the other cited cases.

predicates.appeal_from_supervisory_remand: An appeal concerns a supervisory court's order setting aside a valuation decision and remanding the matter to the assessment tribunal.
predicates.tribunal_excluded_subtenant_rent: The assessment tribunal excluded rent paid by sub-tenants to the tenant when determining annual value.
predicates.valuation_depends_on_multiple_relevant_f: The reasonable annual rental value depends on the owner's rent, sub-tenancy receipts, and other relevant circumstances.

issues.definition: When a supervisory remand follows the tribunal's exclusion of sub-tenancy rent and valuation depends on multiple relevant factors, the tribunal must reconsider the valuation using all relevant circumstances.
